utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the OTP wanted to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there is once matter. But I should have been clear that -- clearer that we should wait until we're in private session for me to raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we even move into closed session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Being in open session, I first now repeat the announcement we made in the closed session that we'll not sit on the 25th of July. That is the last day before the summer recess, as it was scheduled. And the Chamber also sees that Mr. Mladic is back in court and is -- is happy to see that he recovered from his illness. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to examine the witness? Mr. Skrba, you'll now first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for the Defence. Before you do so, Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. Skrba, it's -- it's quite many days ago that you were here for the last time, but I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your appearance before this Court. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here we are in the courtroom after quite a while, so I would like to ask you to say for the record your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name is Milos Skrba.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court whether there was a time after your conversations with the Defence team of General Mladic when you gave our team a written statement.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we call up in e-court 1D1604. This is a 65 ter number. First we need the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give the right number, Mr. Stojanovic, because it may concern another witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat, Your Honours. 65 ter 1D0604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. I will step forward and attempt to assist my counsel here, my fellow counsel. I believe the correct number may be 1D01611, but I will leave it to my learned friend to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we've created some confusion. So let us look at this document together. I believe we now have it. I will repeat the number that I have, 65 ter, unless I am confused: 1D01604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- I'm looking at Annex B to your motion, Mr. Stojanovic. There I find a number, which is the number mentioned by Mr. Shin. Now whether that's the right number or not is a different matter, but let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number you are calling is the number uploaded as the statement of Mr. Batinic, so therefore I suggest that you find a better number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should try 1D1611, as Mr. Shin suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Shin took the risk of interference, but he might have the -- quoted the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. It's possible. If this is the statement of the previous witness, then we have a typo in our notes, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There it is. Let's move on with 1D01611, which is now on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now you see your statement before you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These personal details next to your name, father's name, date of birth, are they correct? And is the signature on this page yours?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at the last page now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that you would upload an English version which really gives the father's names as we find it in the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall do that, Your Honours, presently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you see the last page now of this written statement. Could you tell us, is this again your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today when you gave the solemn declaration stating that you would tell the truth, do you stand by this statement and was it given to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours I would then like to tender 65 ter 01611.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1611 receives number D524, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness, could I ask you whether you're father's name is Simo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I suggest the accompanying documents to be admitted as well, 65 ter 1D02042.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we -- you would continue to list them and as soon as there's any objection, we'll hear there Mr. Shin once you've given the number. Next one would be, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next number would be 65 ter 1D02043; then 1D02044; 65 ter 1D02045; 1D02046; and, finally, 1D02047.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2042 receives number D525. Document 1D2043 receives number D526. Document 1D2044 receives number D527. Document 1D2045 receives number D528. Document 1D2046 receives number D529. And document 1D2047 receives number D530 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D525 up and including D530 [Realtime transcript read in error "D550"] are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With your leave, Your Honours, I should like to present a brief summary of this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Milos Skrba lived and worked in Sarajevo in the neighbourhood of Pofalici before the war. He left his home in fear of daily inspections by the Green Berets. That decision proved to be right because in May 1992 a massacre was perpetrated followed by an exodus of the Serbian population from Pofalici. He joined the VRS close to Petrovici village where he had fled. He assumed the duties of the deputy commander of a company in the 2nd Battalion of the Sarajevo Motorised Brigade and after the commander got killed in the summer of 1992, he took over the duties of company commander in the sector of the road Lukavica-Pale. The witness maintains that his company did not have heavy artillery, that he never received either written or oral orders from the battalion commander to open fire on civilian targets. He personally never issued such an order to his subordinate units. He also speaks about humanitarian convoys that passed unhindered through the territory controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. Concerning the incident marked in our indictment as G-18, Markale II. He says that in August 1995 he was in Studenkovici village, and he's certain that there were no 120-millimetre mortars in that area. Concerning the incident marked in our indictment as F-1. The witness testifies that the feature known as Baba Stijena in the defence area of his company and claims that throughout 1992 or later his company did not have sniper weapons, nor did it ever fire from these positions. Finally, he says that from their positions above Sirokaca they did not have optic visibility of the Sirokaca neighbourhood because at the foot of their positions they could not see the terrain in the Zagrici Street. That is all at this moment, Your Honours. With your leave I should like to put several questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, Mr. Stojanovic, I'd like to state that page 10, line 1, reads as if I would have said D525 up to and including D550 where in my recollection I said 530, but whatever I said, even if it's correctly recorded, then I meant to say 530. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement you mentioned events relative to the movement of humanitarian convoys through -- who moved through the area controlled by the army of Republika Srpska. What territory did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only road in the eastern part of Sarajevo from Pale onto Serbia and to Mostar. That was the only road, the only entry and exit from the eastern part of Sarajevo which was inhabited by civilians, where the VRS were deployed. In other words, the -- both the civilian and military lives took place in that area. Convoys passed through there every day. There was no other road that they could take.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to those humanitarian convoys, were they headed towards the part of Sarajevo which was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In which part of the territory of Sarajevo did they enter the part of Sarajevo which was under the control of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They entered near the airport and in Grbavica. There was a bridge there, the Fraternity and Unity Bridge, where the humanitarian convoys entered -- actually, that what's it was called before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war at any moment as an officer in your company, did you receive an order to either ban the movement of those convoys or to hinder their passage through the area that you controlled?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory that we controlled, our instruction was to allow all the vehicles carrying humanitarian aid to pass through our territory. We did not even control them. There was a police check-point, a military police check-point where they were checked, but what I'm say something is that all the convoys could pass freely through our territory and they regularly did so. As a matter of fact, I'm talking about that part of that road which was under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you also mentioned certain events that took place in May 1992 in Pofalici. What would be your personal knowledge of what happened in May 1992 and involved the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a major exodus of the population because Muslim forces had attacked the majority Serbian population. I wasn't there. I left a bit before on the 4th of April. I had resided there and I saw that the situation was very hard in that part. I had some relatives and friends there who were Serbs, and as you can see from my statement I was right. They faired very badly, they walked for several dozens of kilometres. The situation was beyond words. The words escape me. I can't describe it. I want wasn't there but I heard it from my neighbours who had fled that the situation was really hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to call up D526. I believe that I've got the right number. Unfortunately, we don't have the right document. Let's do it another way. 1D02044, that's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is D527, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the right document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the map. Can you recognise the area that was controlled by your company?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the -- it is well marked in this map from one end to the next and you can see that the area is wooded and rather inaccessible. And when it comes to sniper fire, you can see that it was next to impossible to open sniper fire from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Chamber whether the positions of your company were next to the road that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as you can see it on the map. But our positions were along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the positions of your company, did they come under infantry sniper and artillery attacks during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What did you ask me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Were you exposed by artillery, sniper, and infantry fire by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war from 1992 up to 1995, did your positions move forward or did you retreat from the lines that are marked here?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reached the line in 1992 and we never moved from there before 1995. We were deployed there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have protective fences between the trenches and the positions of your company?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had protective fences on the road itself and also between the trenches. We were not able to communicate -- or if there hadn't been those fences and protective measures installed, we would not have been able to communicate or deliver food to our fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to ask the usher to provide the witness with a blue pencil and I would like to ask the witness to put a circle around the feature that is known as Baba Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. It is in the direction of Trebevic. This curve is what is known as Baba Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put letters BS next to that little blue circle that you just drew.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please try and mark to the best of your recollection as you look -- as you're looking at this map, could you please tell us where Zagrici Street is? If you can find it, could you please encircle it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is below Sirokaca. I'll try to mark it. It is not very clear. However, I would assume that it is somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also see the word Zagrici on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not very clearly, but I would assume that this is the street. If the map can be zoomed in, it would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we can't do anything because we would lose your previous markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, a blue circle in the central part of the image is next to the word "Zagrici."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now before you make an additional marking, are you familiar with the area known as Palez?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the southern part of Trebevic. From the first blue dot, the entire southern slope of Trebevic is covered in shrub. Very stoney, very inaccessible. So there were no war operations going on there ever because the area is hardly accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now place a circle around that general area, the area of Palez as you described it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean -- shall I use the pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now in the middle can you put a letter P.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you again perhaps even spell the name of the area starting with a P which was marked last by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. As I can see on page 15, line 22, and I will spell it: P-a-l-e-z, the last letter is Z and it is pronounced Palez. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question about this document. To the best of your recollection, the distance between the area as you marked it on the map saying that it is called Baba Stijena to Zagrici Street as the crow flies, what is that distance?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be over a thousand metres. I really can't tell you exactly. Our visibility was up to the forest. There is a cemetery there and that was about 800 metres. We could not see any further than that. And there was a cemetery and there were popular trees and other trees. However, as I'm looking at the map, I would say that the distance must be over a thousand metres. Maybe even 1500 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we have a map before us with a scale. I mean, if the witness would say 2 kilometres, that wouldn't change anything on this map, where it is -- I would say, approximately 7-, 800 metres. Now, of course, you have to calculate the difference in altitude. But why not do this in the most accurate way, not relying on a vague impression of someone, but just to focus on what is given as detailed information? And I have another question for you, and also for Mr. Shin, was there any dispute about where this street which was by the way not marked by the witness with a circle but with a dot, Zagrici Street, is there any dispute about where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're just -- because of the scale of this map, we're checking to confirm that that's exactly where it is, but it should be a specific location. There shouldn't be a dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's another matter. Whether we are interested in streets or whether we are interested in houses in those streets, and isn't it true that we have gone through that in extreme detail with -- during the Prosecution's case. Mr. Stojanovic, therefore, if there's any challenge to what was told to us by the witness in the Prosecution's case, then please focus on what that witness said and challenge that rather than to give us a street which may be 100 metres long or 200 metres long and not giving us any further accurate details. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The reason behind that question was the witness's statement or rather the statement of a Prosecution expert who measured the distances. We will have an expert to testify about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to Baba Stijena, Witness, did there come a moment in 1993 -- or rather 1992, when you had sniper weapons and sharpshooters?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not have either a sniper rifles or sharpshooters to handle them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a possibility to have positions on Baba Stijena from which you could open artillery -- infantry fire?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Baba Stijena feature was a very steep rock and it was impossible to have any positions or trenches or features there. To the left -- to the right from that feature we did have trenches from which we opened fire, but Baba Stijena was -- did not lend itself to any defence positions being created there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. I have no further questions to you. I will hand you over to my colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe this is a good moment to tender this map into evidence with the markings made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's D527 but now again marked by the witness would receive, Madam Registrar, number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D531 is admitted into evidence. And before we start the cross-examination -- Witness, could you tell us, you said you were sniped at in your positions. From where were you sniped at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you see the map in front of you. There was some house there is, some civilian features from where they were shooting. There is a part behind this called Debelo Brdo which was under their control. It was a wooded area, it was close by, so they could fire from there. Because in 1992 the road was not protected, then every day we were exposed to these things and we had a lot of casualties, both civilians and troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Debelo Brdo not being on this map? Or is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's not. But I know, more or less, by looking at the map where it is. It's above Cicin Han and you can see this green belt. That's Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have seen maps where Debelo Brdo is indicated. One second, please. You said that it was hardly possible to use your positions as positions from where you could open sniper fire. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly was the reason that you couldn't do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the optical visibility was poor. These forces were well dug in and it was difficult to see them, and we couldn't do much with snipers either. We were a defence unit. We just waited for an attack. We never executed any attacks ourselves. We were permanently in defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there is a difference between not using sniping fire and not being in a position from where you could have used sniper fire. Now, which of the two is it: That you didn't do it; or that you couldn't because of the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't do it and we couldn't because of our position. So for these two reasons we didn't have snipers, we never had them, we never asked for them, and we were never assigned any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to me how can you be sniped at and not be in a position to open sniper fire irrespective of whether you did it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were not the type of unit. And we also had no interest in chasing anyone around in the woods. But it was in their interest to cut off the road that we were using at any cost. So they used all available means, including snipers, to prevent the passage of traffic, of goods, people, along that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But my question is: What you need for sniper fire is a line of sight between the position from where you fire and the target. Could you explain to me how in one direction you could; and in the reverse direction, you couldn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It all depends on the intention of the parties, what they intended and what they wanted. That's the only difference. The difference is in the intent of one side, what it wants to do to the other. And that's why they used it. We didn't have that intention. We didn't have anything to fire at on that side because, really, they didn't also -- they actually had two or three parts where they would cut off the road near Baba Stijena and here in the woods where there would be people passing, so they didn't really have any other room where they could cut it off. So we had to build protective barriers. We had to use planks to build up the cover and different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've given an answer although have not answered my question. But let's leave it to that for the time being. Mr. Shin, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Shin. You'll find Mr. Shin to your right. Mr. Shin is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to begin with some questions about your position in the VRS. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- you explain that you were in the 2nd Infantry Company at the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Smbr. Now, you were appointed company commander in summer of 1992. Could you tell us what your rank was when you were company commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a second-lieutenant in the reserves. I wasn't an active commissioned officer. I was a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just to clarify one point. Before you were made company commander, you were the deputy company commander. Could you tell us when you became deputy company commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became deputy company commander in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was that the first post that you held in the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean, "post"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was that the first position -- did you have a position before you were made deputy company commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I was the deputy, but before that I didn't have any other post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now in your statement, that's paragraph 15, you note that you were "in the command of the 2nd Infantry Battalion." Could you explain that phrase? What -- was that a different position from company commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later in late 1993 where -- I didn't put that down here. I transferred to the battalion command, and I became assistant logistics commander. This was in 1994/1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe just to clarify that, you mentioned late 1993 as well as 1994/1995. When was it that you were actually taking this post in the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in 1993, late 1993, until the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Did your rank change or did you just change position?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My rank changed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you some questions about your company. So this is now going back to the time when you were a company commander. How many platoons were in your company?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And how many soldiers total was that under your command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had about 160. It depends. It varied. There were a lot of troops wounded, killed, especially in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I'm not sure if I should break now or continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this is a suitable --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- moment for you, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now would be a good time, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be brought into the courtroom, first of all, I put on the record, Mr. Shin, that you most likely have received a hard copy of the request you earlier asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could I ask the attention for the following. On the 11th of June, and I'll speak about P3059, on 11th of June the Chamber asked the Prosecution to verify the accuracy of the English translation of Exhibit P3059. On the 17th of June the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence through an informal communication that it is has uploaded the revised translation to e-court under doc ID number 0528-8804-00-ET and requested that this document replace the existing English translation, and the Chamber would like to hear the Defence's position on the new version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, if you are ready, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, just before the break, we were discussing your company when you were company commander in 1992 and 1993. You had just told us that you had 160 men under your command, approximately. You had explained that a little bit as well. Now continuing on this topic, as company commander you issued orders to your platoons with the expectation that they would be followed; correct? That's simply the principle of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And as the company commander, the leader of the company, you were responsible for the safety of your men; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your men in fact looked to you for that, as their commander.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And this is a responsibility you took very seriously, of course; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now part of ensuring the safety of your men, that's situational awareness; meaning, awareness of where your enemy is, awareness of where the VRS units are, and also awareness of units in the field. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And as part of that situational awareness, you would also need to know the activities of your fellow VRS units at a minimum to avoid any inadvertent fire that some armies call friendly fire?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. Part of situational awareness, as we've discussed it, is knowing what the activities of your fellow VRS units in your area; understanding that. That's part of situational awareness, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be. And in most cases we did know that, but not always. We had these natural barriers that would prevent us from knowing exactly what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we'll get into some of that, but for now let me ask you this: To ensure the safety of your men, if your unit needed support from other VRS units, you would naturally ask for that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: From the battalion command. Okay. Now let's turn to your company's zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could have D527 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Skrba, you will recognise it as the document we've just looked at. And --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we can -- we can see -- I'm sorry, were you going to say something?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that when we're talking about the company, the company comprised the reserve troops. And -- just for you -- it to be more clear: These were not professional trained soldiers. These were reserve forces which for the most part were older men, 40 years old and up. Middle-aged men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So this map shows your zone of -- your company's zone of responsibility. And just for -- for reference --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the right side of that. You've drawn a red arrow. That red arrow, that marks the right side of your zone of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: For future reference let's just note that that red arrow begins just above the letter K in a place called Knjeginac. Now -- and we may refer to that precise point later.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Which unit was to your left, to the left of the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Company?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Company. It was also part of the 2nd Battalion, our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And would it be correct to the left of the 3rd Company then was also the 6th Company?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have six companies. Our battalion had four companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. We may get into that a little later on. What unit was to the left of the 3rd Company then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the so-called -- well, it was a different company. It was the 1st Company and the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Which of those two was directly to the left of the 3rd Company?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, do you know somebody named Captain Predrag Trapara?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the name, but he was not in our battalion. He was in a different battalion, not in ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Are you talking about throughout the war or only a very limited time during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was never in our battalion during the entire period of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So if I were to tell that you that he was the commander of the 5th Company in the 2nd Battalion, you don't think that's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander of a company, but this other battalion during the war, we were the 3rd Battalion, and they were the 2nd Battalion, and then for some reason we switched and that's why you're mixing this up. The 1st and the 2nd battalion. At the beginning of the war, they were the 2nd Battalion and we were the 3rd Battalion and later it was changed so then we became the 2nd battalion and they the 3rd. And then it's possible that there were five or more companies in that other battalion, but because I didn't have anything to do with them physically, I don't know. It was a completely separate unit. We had nothing to do with them. It was a different section of the territory than us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe just one question so that at least with respect to your company we're clear: Who was your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain First Class Blagoje Kovacevic was the commander of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was that during the entire period of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the beginning, at the very beginning in 1992. Because we were part of the 1st Romanija Brigade, so until the 1st Sarajevo Brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So after that, who was the commander of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a very short period of time, it was Dragan Vucetic. I don't know if this is mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Dragan Vucetic. And that was a short period of time. And after him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then Blagota Kovacevic came afterwards. Blagoje Kovacevic. In late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And then was he the commander until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn back to this map now to your zone of responsibility. Which unit was to your immediate right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pale unit, but I don't know anything about the establishment. It was a unit from Pale, a company. I didn't communicate with them, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was that part of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Which battalion was it part of?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Pale unit. I don't have the information. I never asked. I wasn't really interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue on here. Now, you assert in your statement - that's paragraph 7 - that the Muslim units facing your company "also had their positions behind the lines exclusively in civilian facilities and houses." Now we'll get more into that issue, but for now I'd just like to focus on where your company was situated on the line -- on your zone of responsibility. In the Karadzic trial - that's transcript 29191 - when you were asked where you got this information about where the Muslim units were situated, you said: "We saw it ourselves." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. We were close together. And then during firing I could see where the fire came from, the fortified bunkers or from the woods. We kept evaluating where the firing was coming from because they kept changing their positions, and we would observe that. You had to know where the firing was coming from. You -- you had to know that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the very last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, could you please repeat the last part of your sentence. The translators were unable to catch that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to know where they fired from, from different weaponry, because we were guarding the feature, the road. Whenever they fired we would locate the origin of the fire, and because we were close together, their trenches and our trenches, we could see their cross-trenches. We could see where they were located, their cross-trenches and trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in fact, in your Karadzic testimony, you went on to say: "Those positions," meaning the Muslim positions, "were so close that they could be observed from our locations. Our positions were better in tactical terms than theirs." You stand by your testimony in the Karadzic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that. I don't know whose positions were better because their positions were in the forest, whereas we were practically on the open road like clay pigeons almost, so we were forced to create barriers, shields, and we dug trenches. We did all sorts of things to protect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, in your Karadzic testimony, you said that your positions, your company's positions were better in tactical terms than those of the Muslim units facing you. Are you changing your testimony now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not changing my testimony, but I'm -- believe that in some way we had more favourable positions because we were on higher ground, on the road; whereas, they were in the forest. Tactically our position was better because we were on the road, while they were in the forest. But as far as combat activities are concerned, they were in a better position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But you acknowledge you were in better tactical positions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some situations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In your statement for the Karadzic case, this is what you said - that will be paragraph 19 of that document, and if we need it, I'll refer to it: "Our positions were tactically better than the Muslim positions and we could have, had we wanted, destroyed them by throwing rocks at them let alone by using weapons." You stand by that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I stand by that. That's the position that I described a moment ago. Our position was better than theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to ask you a little bit about the equipment that your company had, about the weapons that your company had. Now, in the Karadzic case you testified that your company had rifles, including automatic weapons and semi-automatic weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you about a few other pieces of -- some other weapons. Did your company also have M53 machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few. Yes, but very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did your company also have M84 machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, no. Later, towards the end of the year, we received a couple of M84 machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, I'd like to go back to the M53 where the witness said they had them but very few. How many did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the M84, how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two beginning with 1993. At the beginning, we didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, do we understand you correctly that your company did not have any mortars?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Are you aware that there were other infantry companies in the 1st Smbr that did have mortars. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware. But the battalion command must be aware, because they decided which unit, where, should have mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And now that you've told us that you were a staff officer on the battalion command from late 1993, you, too, were aware of that, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the job of operative officers. My job was logistics; supplies, food, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness, witness, could you please answer the question. Not who should be aware; whether you were aware or not. Do I have to understand your answer to be you were not aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew about 82--millimetre mortars, yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then your previous answer was evasive. To say others should know about it where you are specifically asked whether you were aware of mortars, your answer should have been yes, I was aware of 82-millimetre mortars. Could you please keep in mind that telling who should know is not an answer to whether you knew and apparently you were aware. Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, regarding your position in the battalion command, as assistant commander for logistics, that is a position that deals with the resupply of ammunition to the battalion. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, among other things. So during the over two years that were in the battalion command as assistant commander for logistics, you saw that there were 82-millimetre mortar shells and 60-millimetre mortar shells that were being sent to units in the battalion; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- going back to your company and the weapons that your company had, did it have any Osa?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did it have any Zoljas?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had only hand held launchers, RVs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the rest of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry, Mr. Skrba, the translators were unable to hear the remainder of your answer, so if you could please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days we had so-called RVs, hand-held launchers, and grenades for the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to move onto a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And for this, I'd like to pull up a different map. Could I please have D526. I think I have the correct number for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now while we're waiting for this to come up, Mr. Skrba, in your statement, that's paragraph 15, you describe the location of "an 82-millimetre mortar in August of 1995." And you also refer to a map that you marked to show the location of this mortar. Now, do you recognise this to be that map which you had marked to show where this 82-millimetre was? And I'm speaking now of that red circle?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I marked it, and that's the positions called Mala Kula, Little Tower. It was at the foot of that hill which is called Kula, and on top of that hill there were mortars. I don't know how many, but there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, recalling where you had marked on the previous map the right side of your company's zone of responsibility with a red arrow beginning just above the letter K in Knjeginac, could you please tell this Chamber whether this 82-millimetre mortar position was in your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in whose area of responsibility that -- hill was. I'm not sure it was in our area. It was certainly in the area of the battalion. There was a company covering that area, but I didn't have any connection or contact with them. We were directly reporting to the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, just to clarify one thing here, you said that you're not sure whether this was in your zone of responsibility. Does that mean you think it was possible that it was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it wasn't because we had no contact with them. They were subordinated to the battalion command. Since we had no contact, no links, it means that we had no jurisdiction over them, or any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Right. But it's at least very close to your zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the map, it seems relatively close. But if you ever actually go there, you will see that it's quite a distance. Along this winding road, there would be about 2, 3 kilometres to those positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, comparing your marking on D527 with two arrows explaining what your zone of responsibility was, this marking on this map squarely falls within the area marked by the two arrows. So before we spend a lot of other time on -- would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. But I just have to explain to you what kind of terrain it is. If you know that, you will agree with me that it's not our area. It's a cliff. It's very steep. And from the area where my company was, you can't reach them on foot or any other way. And my unit had no business on that hill. That hillock is a part of the slopes of Mount Trebevic, and physically, we are cut off from it by natural barriers, although it looks very close. On the map it looks very close. And it seems like it's in our area of responsibility, but on the ground it looks completely different. A completely different situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The markings were yours. Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, you've told this Court that all you knew about the unit that possessed these 82-millimetre mortars was that it was a company in your battalion. Did we understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't understand me correctly. I don't know if it was a platoon or a company. I don't even know exactly how many mortars there were. I just know that some existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm going to ask you specifically about the time that you were now in the battalion command. So late 1993 to the end of the war. At that point when you were at the battalion command, did you learn which unit this was; and did you learn whether it was a company or a platoon?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't interested. I never asked and nobody ever told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you were at the battalion command. And as you've told us, you were resupplying 82-millimetre shells. But you never knew what this unit was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'll move on. Now I want to focus a little bit more on what you were talking about, the precise location of this 82-millimetre mortar. During your Karadzic testimony you were asked about this. And we'll be going over some of that again. But first as we look at this map, that yellow map that we see sort of arching in a loop over that 82-millimetre mortar position, just to be clear that's the Lukavica-Pale road; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you were asked where this red circle was in relation to that road, and you testified: "Well, it is close to the Velesici road where you go up and down." And that's transcript 29195. And you go on to say that on this map: "It seems that it is not close to the road but it is close to the white road." First of all that part of your testimony from the Karadzic case, do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is correct. First of all, Velesici is on the other side of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The other side of the Miljacka river, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. So maybe there was an error in the Karadzic testimony. Let's take a look at a different map to help us find the precise location of these mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 30795.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Skrba, now this -- well, it's up now so I can ask you. First --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, could we first try to clarify it, what the witness said on page 37, line 11. Mr. Skrba, Mr. Shin took you back to the Karadzic testimony and said: "When you were asked, the red circle where that was in relation to the road, that you testified: 'Well, it is close to the,'" and then it's unclear, "'road where you go up and down." Now, what is road where you go up and down. Does it have a name or how do you refer to that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this map that I have before me right now, I marked it, and that's this section. This winding part of the road leads to the very top of Mount Trebevic. And there is a village there called Medjusi and it's exactly marked Studenkovici village and Medjusi village as well as Blizaci. From this cross-roads 30 to 50 metres away there were mortars, close to the winding section of the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, one second. The winding section of that road. Do you refer to it by any name or is it just the winding section of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It leads to the top of Mount Trebevic. It's just a winding part of the road. It has no name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Skrba, when you were saying that that red circle indicating the 82-millimetre mortars was close to a winding road, are you referring then to the road that connects Studenkovici to the Lukavica-Pale road? I think you've already said yes; is that correct? Mr. Skrba, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The answer by witness "yes" was simply a statement of understanding the question and not the answer to the question because the interpretation was not finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't understand what you asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My question was -- well, basically when you said that the 82-millimetre mortars were near the road going up and down, just so we're clear you're referring to the road that connects Studenkovici to that yellow road, the Lukavica-Pale road?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you didn't quite understand me. This winding road leads to the top of Mount Trebevic. It's the main road. And this other part forks off to Studenkovici village. You see the cross-roads. There is a fork there, one side is the Studenkovici village, the other side leads to the top of Trebevic. From this cross-roads, at a distance of 30 to 50 metres there were 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness. Please proceed, Mr. Shin. At the very end of the answer, we got to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, the red -- these red lines that you've marked on this map during your Karadzic testimony, these mark what you described as earth or dirt roads that you travelled along when you saw that mortar position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in the Karadzic case, and this would be T29197, you were also asked whether these earth roads that you've marked in red were under SRK control during the duration of the conflict. You testified that these were "roads in our territory where you could move freely." You stand by your testimony in the Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Indeed, when you were asked further what kinds of vehicles could move freely along these roads, you testified that "passenger vehicles" could. And you stand by that as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, passenger vehicles. Yes, I stand by that. This winding road could not take any heavy freight vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But you also agreed with the Prosecutor during your Karadzic testimony that you could drive a jeep along those roads. And you stand by that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A jeep is a relatively small car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move onto a different topic so we don't need this map now. In your statement, Mr. Skrba, and that's paragraph 1, you say that you went to the village of Petrovici in April 1992. And after you got there, you say in paragraph 3 that "the local population self-organised and went out on the outskirts of this Serbian village in order to defend their houses." And then you refer to a map where you marked this line of defence. Let's take a look at that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could please have D525. And if we could move to the right side where Trebevic appears and magnify that a little, I'd be grateful. Maybe include a little bit more south of where -- what we have right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A little bit more down --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, just -- yes. We can see the red line now just to the left and slightly above the word Trebevic, and this is what you marked -- so that we're clear, this is what you marked to show that line of defence in that village; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now you were asked also to make further marks on this map during your Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So I would ask if we could please have 65 ter 7 -- 30784. And while we're waiting for that, Your Honours, I had neglected to tender 65 ter 30795, the previous map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30795 receives number P6597.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6597 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, we have --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. The number has six digits, and it should have five. There's no such number in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. I probably misspoke. The map that I'm requesting is 65 ter 30784. And when we have the map up, perhaps we could just blow it up so that we have the full map on the screen but not go to any further detail than that. We do need to look at the full map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, do you recognise this as the same map that we just saw but with further markings on it that you made during your Karadzic testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that's your signature and the date of 22nd October 2012 in the lower right-hand corner; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, at the very bottom just above the letter S in Sarajevo there's a P. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you put that -- you put that there to mark the location of the village of Petrovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, the red line that we see, not that original line of defence line but this additional red marking starting to -- from the right around the middle of the map from the right of a village called Miljevici winding its way down towards the P that you marked to show the road connecting Miljevici to Petrovici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And on this map we can see it passes by the villages Miljevici and Gojkovici, Kozarevici and then to Petrovici which again is marked by that P. You see those [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we please tender 65 ter 30784.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30784 receives number P6598, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6598 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now in order have a better view on Petrovici as well as to see some other features, I'd like to turn to a different map again and again this is one that you saw during your Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 30782. And while that's coming up, Your Honours, you will recognise this map as another map detail from page e-court 54, the Prosecution Exhibit P3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now once again, Mr. Skrba, you recognise in the lower right-hand corner your signature and -- and the date; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: At the bottom part of this map, we see part -- we most of the Cyrillic letters 1st Smbr. And above the letter M, we see the word Petrovici. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, on this map in the upper left we see the village of Miljevici just under the triangular base of the flag with a number 3 on it. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see Miljevici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now looking at these maps it's clear, isn't it, that in order to go to Petrovici from the north you would have to go past Miljevici, you'd have to go past Gojkovici, you'd have to go past Kozarevici; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a lower Miljevici and there's also upper Miljevici, and I arrived in upper Miljevici. You can see it in the map. We'd go through Stanarici but we do not go to Kozarevici because it's below the road, so I go straight to Petrovici. So I have to go through the cross-roads between Kozarevici and Stanarici. Maybe I can do the markings for you, but if not you can follow the black line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, let's try it this way. Mr. Skrba, are you saying that there is a village called Donje Miljevici which is south of Kozarevici?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you see is Miljevici on this map is Donje Miljevici, whereas a -- a furthermore up to the north, and you can't see it on the map, there is a place called Gornji Miljevici which means that there are two villages by the same name. I had to go through Gornji Miljevici to Stanarici and I do not go to Kozarevici at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay, we'll keep this simple. Basically, your statement says that the defence line was on the outskirts of Petrovici but in fact the line that you drew, which we can recall now was next to Miljevici on this map, it's really quite far away, isn't it? It's not on the outskirts of Petrovici as you say.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I said at the outskirts of Petrovici. I knew I said that it was on the outskirts of the Serbian villages closer to Trebevic and that was an area predominantly inhabited by the Serbs, from Miljevici to Knjeginac on the left-hand side. And from that line towards Trebevic it was an area mostly populated by the Serbs. At the beginning of 1992 in April, that's where we organised our patrols and defence lines and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, in any case your defence line is not on the outskirts of Petrovici; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Before we leave this map, just for completeness, in the centre of this map we see a -- what looks like a small triangle and then we see what appears to be "82 mm." Is this again a marking showing where these 82-millimetre mortars were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the markings that I made?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We would tender this map, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do, I just have a question. At line 45 -- page 45, line 1, Mr. Shin you asked the question: "In any case, your defence line is not on the outskirts of Petrovici; that's correct?" He says no. I just want to know, is it no it's not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not correct that the line was on the outskirts of Petrovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the outskirts of Miljevici and you can see that on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would just for completeness refer you to paragraph 3 once again where the witness has stated his position regarding Petrovici and this line of defence on the outskirts of this Serbian village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned to this extract of P3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P6599, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6599 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to move onto another topic, Mr. Skrba. Your company, it's clear it was in the 1st Smbr; correct.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So as a company that would mean, of course, that it was a subordinate unit of the 1st Smbr?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no. It was subordinated to the 2nd Battalion, to the command of the 2nd Battalion, and the battalion command was subordinated to the 1st Motorised Brigade, which was a Sarajevo brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement, paragraph 16, you say: "In my company there were no sharpshooters throughout 1992 as well as in December of 1992 or during the entire period of the war." Let's look at this further. Now you refer to sniper fire from ABiH positions at several points in your statement. And, for example, that's paragraphs 8, 9, and 16. You've also spoken about that a little bit during your direct examination here, and you explain that your unit came under fire from -- under sniper fire from ABiH positions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, did you know a -- can you -- first of all, can you tell us if you knew where the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion was deployed? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my left wing, approximately. To my left. Perhaps a kilometre and a half away from us. So perhaps even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, did you know a platoon commander in that company named Slobodan Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you're confusing battalions. Tusevljak was in the same battalion as Predrag Trapara. He was not in my battalion at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. But you knew -- you knew this Slobodan Tusevljak, platoon commander. Now did you know that as a platoon commander he had sent -- well, let me rephrase that. As a platoon commander in May of 1992 there with a sniper in his unit sent to him by his battalion commander to neutralise ABiH sniper fire. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I met Slobodan Tusevljak after the war. I didn't know him during the war. I didn't know which platoon he was a member of. I don't -- I didn't know what his position was in the defence of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please answer the question. The question was whether you were aware of a sniper sent to the unit under the command of -- could you please assist me, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, commander of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sent by his battalion commander to neutralize ABiH sniper fire. So it's not about all the other things you told us but whether you were aware of this sniper being sent to neutralise ABiH sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't know that. I told you that I didn't even know the man, let alone where he was or what his position was. I only met him after the war when everything was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Skrba, let's try to approach this a different way. Would you agree that a battalion command sending a sniper to a platoon, that that is one effective way of countering sniper fire from your enemy?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not according to me. I don't know. There are different schools of thought. In my view, that wouldn't be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, I'm looking at the clock. I'd suggest we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I'm sorry, I'd missed the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought into the courtroom, I would briefly pay attention to Exhibit D505. On Friday the 13th of June, the Chamber instructed the Registry to attach the B/C/S translation uploaded into e-court under document number ID 1D09-2433 to Exhibit D505, and admitted D505 into evidence. At the same time, the Chamber requested that if the Prosecution had any objections to this translation, it should inform the Chamber within the next two working days. On that same day the Prosecution, by means of an e-mail, informed the Chamber and the Defence that it has no objection to the translation of D505 as it is now in e-court. And that is hereby put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, just before the break we were discussing what would be an effective way of countering sniper fire. Now, I had asked you whether sniper fire is an effective way of countering sniper fire, and you said that you -- you said not according to me. I don't know. Let me try this a different way. Is sniper fire, in your view, an ineffective way of responding to sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I'm not a trained officer, so I cannot comment upon the different ways of countering sniper fire. I can only talk from experience. There are people out there who are active-duty officers who are much better versed in that, and they can tell you what the most appropriate way would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, you were a company commander with 160 lives, lives of your men, their safety in your hands. During 1992 and 1993, you've also told us that your unit was under sniper fire from the ABiH side. Are you telling us that sniper fire is not an effective way of responding to sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have snipers, which is why I don't know. I don't know how to explain that to you. I did not have an opportunity to learn whether that way would be effective or not because we never had snipers. We responded to their fires with what we had, automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, machine-guns. That's how we countered the enemy sniper fire. That's the only thing I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, as a response to the question you put before the break, whether it be would an effective way of count sniper fire from the enemy, the witness explained, had a clear view on the matter, although at the same time he said he didn't know, that there were different schools, et cetera, et cetera. You're asking for an opinion, as a matter of fact. The witness is giving pretty confusing answers. And when asked whether it would be ineffective, he said he wouldn't know. So let's proceed and let's stick to the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, given the fact that your unit was under sniper fire, did it -- did you ever think about asking your battalion command whether you could have snipers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it never occurred to us. The reason was that there was no line of visibility, and we didn't know what to aim at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's move onto a document which you have seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have Prosecution 672. I'm sorry, that's P672.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, while we're waiting for that to come up, maybe I'll start to explain what it is. It's, again, a document that you've seen before during your Karadzic testimony.
